title: Cost and safety
objectives: stop the same text being re-sent on every call
cap what one user can do
recognise a prompt injection and say why it cannot be patched away

steps.instruction: How big is this system prompt?
steps.code:
const system = "You are a study helper. Answer in one sentence.";
console.log(ai.count(system));
steps.after: Twelve tokens, on every single call, forever. That is the thing to notice.
steps.why: Twelve tokens. Small, until you notice it is resent on every single call, forever.

steps.instruction: What did this call use, in and out?
steps.after: Thirteen in, two out. You pay for both, and the input is the bigger half here.
steps.why: Thirteen in, two out. The input is the bigger half here, and most of it is the same every time.

steps.instruction: Look at that input number again, and imagine a hundred users.
body: The system prompt is identical on every call. So is the instruction block, and any examples you included.
All of it is re-sent, re-read, and re-charged, every time.
On a real app that stable part is often the majority of what you send.
steps.keypoint: The unchanging part of your prompt is sent again on every single call.

steps.instruction: So you mark it, and it gets reused instead of re-read. That is caching.
body: The rule is that a cache matches from the start of the prompt forwards.
So stable content goes first, and anything that changes goes last.
steps.keypoint: Stable content first, changing content last. That order is what makes a cache work.

steps.instruction: This prompt will never hit the cache. Tap the line that ruins it.
steps.why: The timestamp changes every call and it sits at the front, so the very first tokens differ every time and nothing after them can match. Move it to the end, or drop it, and the whole system prompt becomes cacheable.
steps.after: One well-meaning debug line in front of the prompt, and the cache never hits once.
steps.keypoint: Anything that changes belongs at the end. In front, it poisons everything behind it.

steps.instruction: Three different controls, three different jobs. People mix them up constantly.

rows: a loop, or one person hammering it

body: max_tokens does nothing about a user sending a thousand requests.
A rate limit does nothing about one enormous request.
You need all three, and they are each about four lines.
steps.keypoint: Cap the reply, cap the request, cap the user. Three separate controls.

steps.instruction: The question is 800 characters. What does the guard print?
steps.after: Checked before sending, so the huge one never becomes a call at all.
steps.why: Rejected, before it became a call. A size check costs nothing and stops the request that costs a lot.

steps.instruction: The eleventh call in a minute. What does the user get?
steps.after: This app does the same thing: 240 checks a minute per student, to stop a loop, not to ration normal work.
steps.why: Ten allowed, eleventh refused. Enough to stop a runaway loop, not enough to bother anyone working normally.

steps.instruction: Now the one that is not about money. Read this user's note carefully.
body: You built a prompt out of your instruction plus their text. To the model it is all just one block of tokens.
It cannot tell which sentences came from you and which came from a stranger.
That is a prompt injection, and it needs no hacking at all. It is typing.
steps.keypoint: Your instructions and the user's text arrive as one block. Nothing marks which is which.

steps.instruction: Tap the line where the user's text becomes part of your instructions.
steps.why: Gluing them together is the moment the boundary disappears. After that line there is no way for the model, or for you, to tell instruction from input.
steps.after: Every app that puts user text in a prompt has this. Yours will too.
steps.keypoint: The moment you concatenate, the boundary is gone.

steps.instruction: You cannot patch this away. So you build for it.

rules.text: Limit what the model is allowed to do, not what the user is allowed to say.
rules.example: it can suggest a tag, it cannot delete a row

rules.text: Never put secrets in the prompt. Anything in there can come back out.
rules.example: no keys, no other users' data

rules.text: Treat every reply as text from a stranger.
rules.example: never render it as raw HTML

body: Filters for phrases like ignore your instructions are worth little. There are endless ways to say it.
The durable defence is that a successful injection still cannot do anything worth doing.
steps.keypoint: You cannot stop the input. You can make sure a bad input cannot do damage.

steps.instruction: Deal each one into how much trust it has earned.

items.text: the reply, shown as plain text
a tag it chose, from your fixed list
a summary shown under the note

steps.after: Plain text a person reads is fine. Anything your code acts on is checked first.
steps.keypoint: Text for people, unchecked. Values for code, always checked.

steps.instruction: Rate checked, size checked, then send.
steps.after: Under the rate limit, but far too long. Caught before it cost a call.
body: Under the limit, but far too long. Caught before it cost anything.
